record.paper_title: Exchange Bias and Interface-related Effects in Two-dimensional van der Waals Magnetic Heterostructures: Open Questions and Perspectives
record.original_question: How does the type of antiferromagnetic ordering in the antiferromagnetic layer affect exchange-bias behavior in ferromagnet/antiferromagnet van der Waals systems?

evidence.quote: iv. Does type of AFM ordering affect the EB behavior in FM/AFM vdW systems?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a magnetic heterostructure consisting of a two-dimensional van der Waals ferromagnetic (FM) layer placed in contact with a two-dimensional van der Waals antiferromagnetic (AFM) layer. The exchange-bias (EB) effect refers to a horizontal shift H_E of the FM hysteresis loop along the magnetic-field axis after the heterostructure is field-cooled through the Néel temperature of the AFM layer; this shift originates from the interfacial exchange coupling between uncompensated AFM moments and the FM magnetization.

Antiferromagnetic order in a van der Waals layered material can take several distinct forms, including: 
(a) A-type ordering (ferromagnetic intralayer alignment with antiferromagnetic interlayer stacking), 
(b) C-type ordering (antiferromagnetic intralayer chains with ferromagnetic interlayer stacking), 
(c) G-type ordering (antiferromagnetic alignment with all nearest neighbors), 
(d) zigzag, stripy, or Néel intralayer orderings on the honeycomb lattice, 
(e) noncollinear or helical orderings.

Determine quantitatively how the type of antiferromagnetic ordering in the AFM layer governs the exchange-bias behavior of the FM/AFM van der Waals heterostructure. Specifically:

1. Derive, from a microscopic spin Hamiltonian for the FM/AFM interface (including Heisenberg exchange, single-ion anisotropy, and interfacial coupling J_int), the dependence of the exchange-bias field H_E, the coercivity enhancement ΔH_c, and the blocking temperature T_B on the AFM ordering type listed above.

2. In particular, predict (i) for which ordering types H_E remains finite down to the monolayer or bilayer AFM limit, (ii) how the sign of H_E depends on the parity of AFM layers for A-type ordering, and (iii) how intralayer compensated versus uncompensated interfaces (as determined by the ordering type and crystallographic termination) modify the magnitude of H_E.

3. Provide a criterion, in terms of the AFM ordering wavevector and the FM/AFM lattice mismatch, that determines whether a robust exchange-bias effect can be observed.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of how AFM ordering type controls exchange-bias in 2D vdW FM/AFM heterostructures remains an actively investigated open problem. Recent works report material-specific results — e.g., A-type AFM CrPS4/Fe3GeTe2 retains EB down to a bilayer AFM, MnPS3/Fe3GeTe2 shows EB linked to weak ferromagnetic ordering, and CrSBr-based stacks display orthogonal-coupling-induced EB — but no unified theoretical framework relating AFM ordering type to EB magnitude, sign, and blocking temperature has been established.

status_evidence.title: Exchange Bias Effect in Ferro-/Antiferromagnetic van der Waals Heterostructures
status_evidence.snippet: A-type AFM CrPS4 retains EB down to bilayer AFM in Fe3GeTe2/CrPS4 heterostructure, vanishing at single-layer limit.
status_evidence.claim: AFM ordering type and thickness regulate EB persistence in vdW heterostructures.

status_evidence.title: Identifying the Origin of Thermal Modulation of Exchange Bias in MnPS3/Fe3GeTe2
status_evidence.snippet: Exchange bias magnitude linked to anomalous weak ferromagnetic ordering in MnPS3 below 40 K; ~170 mT EB at 5 K.
status_evidence.claim: Different AFM orderings produce qualitatively distinct EB phenomenology, still under active study.

status_evidence.title: Switchable Exchange Bias from Correlated Domain Structures in Orthogonally Coupled AFM/FM vdW Heterostructures
status_evidence.snippet: In-plane AFM state of CrSBr promotes stripe-like FGT domains producing asymmetric switching and EB.
status_evidence.claim: AFM ordering geometry (orthogonal vs collinear) crucially affects EB; field of study still evolving in 2025.
